claim: High AGR2 expression was only observed in lung tumor cell lines (A549, H23, H1838) compared to a non-tumorigenic human bronchial epithelial cell (HBEC).
source: High AGR2 expression was only observed in lung tumor cell lines (A549, H23, H1838) compared to a non-tumorigenic human bronchial epithelial cell (HBEC) (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1A-B) and Western blot analysis (Figure 1C) showing AGR2 expression levels across different cell lines.

claim: The expression pattern of AGR2 in tumor and non-tumor bronchial organoids was similar to that observed in 2D culture.
source: Moreover, the expression pattern of AGR2 in tumor and non-tumor bronchial organoids (Figure 1D) was similar to that observed in 2D culture (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images comparing AGR2 expression in 2D culture (Figure 1A) and 3D organoids (Figure 1D).

claim: AGR2 was overexpressed in tumors compared to adjacent non-tumor tissue.
source: Immunohistochemistry of AGR2 in a cohort of 34 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients (Supplementary file 1A) revealed that AGR2 was overexpressed in tumors compared to adjacent non-tumor tissue (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from 34 NSCLC patients showing differential AGR2 expression between tumor and normal tissue (Figure 1E).

claim: AGR2 expression was essentially restricted to type II pneumocytes in NSCLC tissues.
source: Consequently, AGR2 expression was increased in NSCLC tissues (Figure 1E), and was essentially restricted to type II pneumocytes (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by dual color multiplex immunostaining showing AGR2 and TTF-1 co-localization in type II pneumocytes (Figure 1F).

claim: High AGR2 expression correlated with low survival rate in NSCLCs patients.
source: High AGR2 expression correlated with low survival rate and the low/intermediate AGR2 expression with high survival rate in NSCLCs patients (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showing differential survival based on AGR2 expression levels (Figure 1G, p=0.0138).

claim: Cell growth was strongly inhibited in Sh-AGR2 cells compared to control cells.
source: Cell growth was strongly inhibited in Sh-AGR2 cells compared to control cells (Sh-ctl) (Figure 2C,F,I–J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with no cell death detected (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth curves, BrdU incorporation assays, and Trypan blue exclusion assays showing reduced proliferation without increased cell death.

claim: Soft-agar colony formation significantly reduced upon AGR2 silencing in adenocarcinoma cell lines.
source: Interestingly, soft-agar colony formation (Figure 2L–N) (used as indicator of malignant transformation) significantly reduced upon AGR2 silencing in adenocarcinoma cell lines, thereby indicating that AGR2 may favor tumor progression by increasing anchorage-independent growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by soft agar colony formation assays showing reduced colony numbers in AGR2-depleted cells (Figure 2L-N).

claim: AGR2 silencing dramatically decreased the formation of tumor organoids.
source: AGR2 silencing dramatically decreased the formation of tumor organoids (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by brightfield microscopy and quantification of organoid numbers in 3D culture (Figure 3A-C).

claim: AGR2 depletion significantly reduced total metastasis number (by ~50%) in both A549-Sh-AGR2 and H1838-Sh-AGR2 injected mice.
source: Moreover, AGR2 depletion significantly reduced total metastasis number (by ~50%) in both A549-Sh-AGR2 and H1838-Sh-AGR2 injected mice (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo tail vein injection experiments with quantification of lung metastases in immunodeficient mice (Figure 3D-G).

claim: Overexpression of AGR2 in cancer cells increases their tumorigenic and metastatic potential.
source: Taken together, these results show that overexpression of AGR2 in cancer cells increases their tumorigenic and metastatic potential.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including soft agar assays, organoid formation, and in vivo metastasis experiments.

claim: AGR2 co-localized with calnexin (CANX), an ER resident type I integral membrane protein in HBEC-AGR2 cells.
source: In HBEC-AGR2 cells, AGR2 co-localized with calnexin (CANX), an ER resident type I integral membrane protein (Figure 4B, top panels) and BiP (GRP78), a soluble HSP70 molecular chaperone located in the lumen of the ER (Figure 4B, middle panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence co-localization studies showing AGR2 overlapping with ER markers (Figure 4B).

claim: AGR2 did not co-localize with GM130, a cis-Golgi marker.
source: In contrast and as expected, AGR2 did not co-localize with GM130, a cis-Golgi marker (Figure 4B, bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing lack of co-localization between AGR2 and GM130 (Figure 4B).

claim: AGR2 overexpression enhanced cell proliferation.
source: Remarkably, AGR2 overexpression enhanced cell proliferation (Figure 4D–G) and increased the formation of organoids (Figure 4H), thereby indicating that the expression of AGR2 dictates organoid-initiating frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth curves, BrdU incorporation assays, and organoid formation assays in AGR2-overexpressing cells (Figure 4D-H).

claim: eAGR2 was detected in the extracellular medium of adenocarcinoma organoids (Sh-ctl), but not in adenocarcinoma organoids silenced for AGR2 (Sh-AGR2).
source: Indeed, eAGR2 was detected in the extracellular medium of adenocarcinoma organoids (Sh-ctl), but not in adenocarcinoma organoids silenced for AGR2 (Sh-AGR2) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis of conditioned medium from organoids (Figure 5A).

claim: eAGR2 was secreted in the extracellular medium from HEBC-AGR2 organoids.
source: Similarly, we found that eAGR2 was secreted in the extracellular medium from HEBC-AGR2 organoids (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot detection of AGR2 in extracellular medium from AGR2-overexpressing organoids (Figure 5B).

claim: None of the ER resident proteins Calnexin (CANX) and BiP/GRP78 were detected in the extracellular medium.
source: We also tested the presence of two other proteins of the secretory pathway: Calnexin (CANX) and BiP/GRP78 (Figure 5B). None of these ER resident proteins were detected in the extracellular medium (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis showing absence of CANX and BiP in extracellular medium (Figure 5B).

claim: In adenocarcinoma organoids (H23), there was ~20% of eAGR2 and ~80% of iAGR2.
source: In adenocarcinoma organoids (H23), we found ~20% of eAGR2 and ~80% of iAGR2 (Figure 5D), while in non-tumor organoids (HBEC-EV), AGR2 protein was exclusively intracellular (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and quantification of AGR2 from intracellular and extracellular compartments (Figure 5C-D).

claim: AGR2 overexpression in non-tumor organoids (HBEC-AGR2) forced the secretion of eAGR2 (~30% in the extracellular medium).
source: In contrast, AGR2 overexpression in non-tumor organoids (HBEC-AGR2) forced the secretion of eAGR2 (~30% in the extracellular medium) (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of intracellular versus extracellular AGR2 in overexpressing organoids (Figure 5D).

claim: AGR2 depletion had no impact on BiP and CANX expression.
source: Results showed that of AGR2 depletion had no impact on BiP and CANX expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis comparing BiP and CANX levels in AGR2-depleted versus control organoids (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: After 8 hr of CHX treatment, eAGR2 was practically undetectable, whereas ~60% of iAGR2 was still present.
source: After 8 hr of CHX treatment, eAGR2 was practically undetectable (Figure 5G–H), whereas ~60% of iAGR2 was still present.
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide pulse-chase experiments with immunoprecipitation and quantification of AGR2 (Figure 5G-H).

claim: The KTEL motif of AGR2 stems out of the core protein and has no interaction with the rest of the protein.
source: Structural analysis of AGR2 showed that the KTEL motif stemmed out of the core protein and had no interaction with the rest of the protein.
evidence: The claim is based on structural modeling analysis of AGR2 (Figure 5I).

claim: The NH3+ group of K172 forms a very clear salt bridge to the C-terminal carboxylic group of L175, which yields a stable 'hook' shape.
source: Residue interactions within the KTEL motif are seen more clearly: the NH3+ group of K172 forms a very clear salt bridge to the C-terminal carboxylic group of L175, which yields a stable 'hook' shape (Figure 5I, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis showing specific molecular interactions within the KTEL motif (Figure 5I).

claim: None of the different KTEL motif mutants displayed a specific intracellular localization and all were secreted.
source: Therefore, none of our different KTEL motif mutants displayed a specific intracellular localization and all were secreted.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments testing secretion of various KTEL mutants (KDEL, K172D, K172A, ΔKTEL) in HEK293T cells (Figure 5J-K).

claim: AGR2 secretion results from high iAGR2 expression levels and is not a consequence of cell death or 'leak' of ER proteins into the extracellular medium.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that eAGR2 protein is secreted in the extracellular medium, independently of its KTEL motif and most likely as a soluble protein (eAGR2). AGR2 secretion results from high iAGR2 expression levels and is not a consequence of cell death or 'leak' of ER proteins into the extracellular medium.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing specific AGR2 secretion without secretion of other ER proteins and without cell death.

claim: AGR2 was only detected in the ECM derived from HBEC-AGR2 cell.
source: Western blotting revealed the presence of the ECM component laminin in both HBEC-EV and HBEC-AGR2 cell-derived matrices (Figure 5M), however AGR2 was only detected in the ECM derived from HBEC-AGR2 cell (Figure 5M).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis of purified cell-derived ECM showing AGR2 presence only in AGR2-overexpressing cells (Figure 5M).

claim: Immunofluorescence staining for AGR2 revealed the presence of eAGR2 in the ECM of HBEC-AGR2 cells.
source: As expected, immunofluorescence staining for AGR2 revealed the presence of eAGR2 in the ECM of HBEC-AGR2 cells (Figure 5N, lower panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy of cell-derived ECM showing AGR2 staining (Figure 5N).

claim: The addition of recombinant human AGR2 (40 ng/ml) to the medium of AGR2-depleted tumor cell lines reversed the cell growth inhibition induced by AGR2 depletion.
source: Remarkably, the addition of recombinant human AGR2 (40 ng/ml) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F) to the medium of AGR2-depleted tumor cell lines reversed the cell growth inhibition induced by AGR2 depletion (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting experiments showing rescue of proliferation upon addition of exogenous AGR2 (Figure 6A).

claim: The addition of eAGR2 to the ECM of AGR2-depleted organoids restored the formation of tumor organoids.
source: Moreover, the addition of eAGR2 to the ECM of AGR2-depleted organoids restored the formation of tumor organoids (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays showing rescue of organoid numbers upon addition of recombinant AGR2 (Figure 6B-C).

claim: The addition of the human recombinant AGR2-ΔKTEL (40 ng/ml) to the extracellular medium of AGR2-depleted organoids was still able to restore the formation of tumor organoids.
source: Remarkably, the addition of the human recombinant AGR2-ΔKTEL (40 ng/ml) to the extracellular medium of AGR2-depleted organoids was still able to restore the formation of tumor organoids (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays using AGR2-ΔKTEL mutant protein (Figure 6D).

claim: The KTEL motif is not necessary for eAGR2 extracellular activity.
source: Therefore, the KTEL motif is not necessary for eAGR2 extracellular activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing that AGR2-ΔKTEL can restore organoid formation (Figure 6D).

claim: AGR2-AXXA mutant, in the ECM of AGR2-depleted organoids, did not restore the formation of tumor organoids.
source: AGR2-AXXA mutant, in the ECM of AGR2-depleted organoids, did not restore the formation of tumor organoids (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays showing no rescue with AGR2-AXXA mutant (Figure 6F).

claim: AGR2-SXXS mutant restored the formation of AGR2-depleted tumor organoids.
source: Thus, we used another inactive form of AGR2 thioredoxin-like domain, the AGR2-SXXS mutant. In contrast to the AGR2-AXXA mutant, AGR2-SXXS mutant restored the formation of AGR2-depleted tumor organoids (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays showing rescue with AGR2-SXXS mutant (Figure 6G).

claim: The single cysteine residue in the AGR2 thioredoxin-like domain is not essential for the formation of tumor organoids.
source: These results show that the single cysteine residue in the AGR2 thioredoxin-like domain is not essential for the formation of tumor organoids.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AGR2-SXXS (lacking the active cysteine) can restore organoid formation (Figure 6G).

claim: The addition of DTT to the medium of AGR2-depleted H23 cells neither reversed the cell growth inhibition induced by AGR2 depletion nor restored the formation of tumor organoids.
source: The addition of DTT to the medium of AGR2-depleted H23 cells neither reversed the cell growth inhibition induced by AGR2 depletion (Figure 6I) nor restored the formation of tumor organoids (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth and organoid formation assays with DTT treatment (Figure 6I-J).

claim: Treating cells with reducing agent cannot mimic the effects of eAGR2.
source: Thus, these results demonstrate that treating cells with reducing agent cannot mimic the effects of eAGR2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing DTT cannot rescue AGR2 depletion phenotypes (Figure 6H-J).

claim: eAGR2 enhanced organoid growth ten-fold in non-tumorigenic HBEC.
source: As expected, eAGR2 enhanced organoid growth ten-fold (Figure 6K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of organoid numbers in HBEC treated with recombinant AGR2 (Figure 6K).

claim: Conditioned media from HBEC-AGR2 stimulates the formation of non-tumorigenic organoids eight-fold.
source: Conditioned media from control (HBEC-EV) did not significantly stimulate the formation of HBEC organoids. In contrast, conditioned media from HBEC-AGR2 stimulates the formation of non-tumorigenic organoids eight-fold (Figure 6L).
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays using conditioned media from AGR2-overexpressing cells (Figure 6L).

claim: eAGR2 secreted by organoids and the bacterially expressed human recombinant AGR2 are both active and have the same role on the organoid growth.
source: This demonstrated that eAGR2 secreted by organoids and the bacterially expressed human recombinant AGR2 are both active and have the same role on the organoid growth (Figure 6K–L).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing effects of conditioned media and recombinant AGR2 on organoid formation (Figure 6K-L).

claim: AGR2-ΔKTEL overexpression increased the formation of organoids.
source: AGR2-ΔKTEL overexpression increased the formation of organoids (Figure 6M), thereby confirming that the expression of AGR2 dictates organoid-initiating frequency through an autocrine/paracrine manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays in cells overexpressing AGR2-ΔKTEL (Figure 6M).

claim: eAGR2 extracellular functions were independent of its thioredoxin-like domain and occurred through an autocrine/paracrine manner on organoid-initiating frequency.
source: These results demonstrate that eAGR2 extracellular functions were independent of its thioredoxin-like domain and occurred through an autocrine/paracrine manner on organoid-initiating frequency, a phenotype of transformed tumor cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments with AGR2 mutants, conditioned media, and recombinant proteins.

claim: The apical marker GM130 was randomly distributed throughout the HBEC organoids in presence of eAGR2 in the ECM, in contrast to its restriction to the apical localization in HBEC organoids in the absence of eAGR2.
source: As shown in Figure 7A and B (bottom and right panels), the apical marker GM130 was randomly distributed throughout the HBEC organoids in presence of eAGR2 in the ECM, in contrast to its restriction to the apical localization in HBEC organoids in the absence of eAGR2 (Figure 7A and B (top and left panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and fluorescence intensity profiling showing GM130 redistribution upon eAGR2 treatment (Figure 7A-B).

claim: Control HBEC organoids exhibited a lumen lined by the tight junction marker ZO-1, whereas ZO-1 was no longer restricted to the lumen compartment upon eAGR2 exposure.
source: Similarly, control HBEC organoids exhibited a lumen lined by the tight junction marker ZO-1 (Figure 7C and D; top and left panels), whereas ZO-1 was no longer restricted to the lumen compartment upon eAGR2 exposure (Figure 7C and D; bottom and right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and fluorescence intensity profiling showing ZO-1 redistribution upon eAGR2 treatment (Figure 7C-D).

claim: eAGR2 in the ECM resulted in a disruption of apicobasal polarity of non-tumorigenic organoids.
source: Thus, eAGR2 in the ECM, resulted in a disruption of apicobasal polarity, of non-tumorigenic organoids.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of GM130 and ZO-1 redistribution in eAGR2-treated organoids.

claim: The presence of eAGR2, at the time of plating, gave rise to organoids unable to form a lumen.
source: The presence of eAGR2, at the time of plating, gave rise to organoids unable to form a lumen (+ eAGR2) (Figure 7E–G) thereby showing that eAGR2 interferes with the formation of hollow organoid.
evidence: The claim is supported by F-actin staining and quantification of lumen formation in organoids treated with eAGR2 (Figure 7E-G).

claim: eAGR2 in the ECM induced loss of cell polarity and lumen formation.
source: Collectively, these data provide further evidence that eAGR2, in the ECM, induced loss of cell polarity and lumen formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations of polarity marker redistribution and lumen loss in eAGR2-treated organoids.

claim: eAGR2 resulted in a disruption of cell-cell contact of non-tumorigenic organoids.
source: Thus, eAGR2 in the ECM, resulted in a disruption of cell-cell contact, of non-tumorigenic organoids.
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunofluorescence showing relocalization of E-cadherin, β-catenin, and Laminin-V from cell-cell contacts to cytoplasm (Figure 8A-C).

claim: The addition of eAGR2 to the organoids ECM significantly modified EMT transcripts such as Wnt5b (~thirteen-fold), MMP3 (~eleven-fold), MAP1B (~ten-fold), MMP9 (~eight-fold), ZEB1 (~three-fold), and VIM (~two-fold).
source: The addition of eAGR2 to the organoids ECM significantly modified EMT transcripts such as Wnt5b (~thirteen-fold), MMP3 (~eleven-fold), MAP1B (~ten-fold), MMP9 (~eight-fold), ZEB1 (~three-fold), and VIM (~two-fold) (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR array analysis showing differential gene expression in eAGR2-treated organoids (Figure 9A).

claim: eAGR2 treatment induced Vimentin (VIM), MMP9 and N-Cadherin (CDH2) expression and decreased E-Cadherin (CDH1) expression at the protein level.
source: These results were also confirmed at the protein level with the induction of Vimentin (VIM), MMP9 and N-Cadherin (CDH2) expression upon treatment with eAGR2 as well as decreased E-Cadherin (CDH1) expression (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis showing changes in EMT marker protein levels upon eAGR2 treatment (Figure 9C).

claim: eAGR2 disrupted laminin layers to invasive structures.
source: These experiments showed that eAGR2 disrupted laminin layers to invasive structures (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing loss of laminin at the basement membrane in eAGR2-treated organoids (Figure 9D).

claim: A cell invasion phenotype correlates with the presence of eAGR2 in the ECM of non-tumorigenic organoids.
source: Hence, we correlate a cell invasion phenotype with the presence of eAGR2 in the ECM of non-tumorigenic organoids.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of invasive structures and laminin disruption in eAGR2-treated organoids (Figure 9D).

claim: AGR2 is retained in the ER through a mechanism involving its KTEL motif and the three KDEL receptors.
source: AGR2 is retained in the ER through a mechanism involving its KTEL motif and the three KDEL receptors (Gupta et al., 2012; Alanen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on AGR2 ER retention mechanisms.

claim: eAGR2 secretion is independent of the KTEL sequence and is not a consequence of cell death or 'leaky' release of ER proteins into the extracellular medium.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that eAGR2 secretion is independent of the KTEL sequence and, is not a consequence of cell death or "leaky" release of ER proteins into the extracellular medium.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing specific AGR2 secretion without other ER proteins and without cell death.

claim: The production of AGR2 is linked to the amount of secreted eAGR2.
source: Hence, our data show that the production of AGR2 is linked to the amount of secreted eAGR2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from cycloheximide experiments showing reduced eAGR2 upon blocking AGR2 synthesis.

claim: High levels of eAGR2 could directly contribute to the tumorigenecity of tumor cells.
source: Moreover, high levels of eAGR2 could directly contribute to the tumorigenecity of tumor cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on observations of AGR2 secretion and tumor phenotypes.

claim: AGR2 depletion in cancer cells significantly decreased tumor cell proliferation.
source: Indeed, AGR2 depletion in cancer cells significantly decreased tumor cell proliferation, suggesting that high levels AGR2 in tumor cells is important for sustaining tumor cell growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assays in AGR2-depleted cells (Figure 2).

claim: Restoration of eAGR2 in the microenvironment of AGR2-knockdown tumor cells reversed AGR2 depletion-induced cell growth inhibition.
source: Furthermore, our data show that restoration of eAGR2 in the microenvironment of AGR2-knockdown tumor cells reversed AGR2 depletion-induced cell growth inhibition and thus indicate that the reduced cell proliferation induced by AGR2 depletion is most likely due to the reduction of eAGR2 in the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments with recombinant AGR2 (Figure 6A).

claim: The reduced tumor organoids formation in AGR2-depleted cells can be restored by addition of exogenous eAGR2.
source: This is independent of iAGR2 since the reduced tumor organoids formation in AGR2-depleted cells can be restored by addition of exogenous eAGR2.
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays with recombinant AGR2 (Figure 6B-C).

claim: For the eAGR2 extracellular activity, the KTEL motif is not required.
source: Our data reveal that for the eAGR2 extracellular activity, the KTEL motif is not required.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing AGR2-ΔKTEL can restore organoid formation (Figure 6D).

claim: Tumor organoid formation was restored when AGR2-depleted tumor organoids were supplemented with AGR2-SXXS (thioredoxin inactive), but not in the presence of reducing agent.
source: Remarkably,, tumor organoid formation was restored when AGR2-depleted tumor organoids were supplemented with AGR2-SXXS (thioredoxin inactive), but not in the presence of reducing agent
evidence: The claim is supported by organoid formation assays with AGR2-SXXS mutant and DTT treatment (Figure 6G, 6J).

claim: eAGR2 drives tumor organoids formation through its presence within the ECM, not by changing the redox nature of microenvironment.
source: Therefore, our data demonstrate that eAGR2 drives tumor organoids formation, not by changing the redox nature of microenvironment but through its presence within the ECM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing AGR2-SXXS activity and lack of DTT effect.

claim: eAGR2 has a crucial biological function in the tumorigenesis of cancer cells.
source: Our experiments provide the first evidence that eAGR2 has a crucial biological function in the tumorigenesis of cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing eAGR2 effects on tumor cell properties.

claim: Overexpressing AGR2 enhanced cell proliferation and increased the formation of organoids in human bronchial epithelial non-tumor cells.
source: We found that overexpressing AGR2 enhanced cell proliferation and increased the formation of organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation and organoid formation assays in AGR2-overexpressing HBEC (Figure 4D-H).

claim: The presence of eAGR2 in the ECM was sufficient to impact on cell's autocrine/paracrine signaling to in turn enhance organoid-initiating frequency.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that the presence of eAGR2 in the ECM was sufficient to impact on cell's autocrine/paracrine signaling to in turn enhance organoid-initiating frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with recombinant AGR2 and conditioned media (Figure 6K-L).

claim: In the presence of eAGR2 in the ECM, HBECs form large, non-polarized, undifferentiated organoids without lumen, therefore mimicking tumor organoids.
source: In normal conditions, HBECs form polarized and spherical organoids with hollow lumens, however in the presence of eAGR2 in the ECM, these identical cells form large, non-polarized, undifferentiated organoids without lumen, therefore mimicking tumor organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy showing loss of polarity markers and lumen formation in eAGR2-treated organoids (Figure 7).

claim: eAGR2 alone is sufficient to confer a tumorigenic phenotype in non-tumor organoids.
source: Hence, eAGR2 alone is sufficient to confer a tumorigenic phenotype in non-tumor organoids.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that eAGR2 treatment induces tumor-like characteristics in normal organoids.

claim: eAGR2 promotes a cell invasion phenotype characterized by the disruption of basal laminin.
source: We demonstrated that eAGR2: i) promotes a cell invasion phenotype characterized by the disruption of basal laminin and, ii) disrupts cell-cell contact characterized by the loss of E-cadherin, β-catenin and Laminin-V at the cell membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing laminin disruption and invasive structures in eAGR2-treated organoids (Figure 9D).

claim: eAGR2 disrupts cell-cell contact characterized by the loss of E-cadherin, β-catenin and Laminin-V at the cell membrane.
source: We demonstrated that eAGR2: i) promotes a cell invasion phenotype characterized by the disruption of basal laminin and, ii) disrupts cell-cell contact characterized by the loss of E-cadherin, β-catenin and Laminin-V at the cell membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing relocalization of adhesion molecules in eAGR2-treated organoids (Figure 8).

claim: eAGR2 triggers the induction of Vimentin and N-Cadherin.
source: Moreover, eAGR2 triggers the induction of Vimentin and N-Cadherin.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis showing increased Vimentin and N-Cadherin expression upon eAGR2 treatment (Figure 9C).

claim: Expression of mesenchymal markers, together with the loss of E-cadherin and β-catenin from cell–cell contacts, as well as the invasive behavior of the organoids suggests that the non-tumorigenic epithelial cells were converted from an epithelial to a mesenchymal phenotype in presence of eAGR2 in their ECM.
source: Expression of these mesenchymal markers, together with the loss of E-cadherin and β-catenin from cell–cell contacts, as well as the invasive behavior of the organoids suggests that the non-tumorigenic epithelial cells were converted from an epithelial to a mesenchymal phenotype in presence of eAGR2 in their ECM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations of EMT markers and phenotypes in eAGR2-treated organoids.

claim: eAGR2 in ECM is sufficient by itself to induce EMT in non-tumor epithelial cells.
source: Although it has been only correlated that AGR2 may stimulate EMT, it is intriguing to find that eAGR2 in ECM is sufficient by itself, to induce EMT in non-tumor epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR array and Western blot data showing EMT marker changes in eAGR2-treated organoids (Figure 9).

claim: eAGR2 is important for epithelial morphogenesis disruption and metastatic dissemination.
source: Together, our results indicate that eAGR2 is important for epithelial morphogenesis disruption and metastatic dissemination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing eAGR2 effects on polarity, invasion, and EMT.

claim: eAGR2 is a microenvironmental regulator of epithelial tissue architecture, which has a role in the preneoplastic phenotype and thus, contributes to tumorigenicity in epithelial cells.
source: In conclusion, the findings from the present study demonstrate that eAGR2 is a microenvironmental regulator of epithelial tissue architecture, which has a role in the preneoplastic phenotype and thus, contributes to tumorigenicity in epithelial cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the totality of experimental evidence showing eAGR2 effects on normal and tumor cells.

claim: eAGR2 present in the ECM of non-tumorigenic organoids is sufficient, by itself, to disrupt cell polarization and organoid formation, thus leading to a disorganized phenotype with invasive properties.
source: Indeed, eAGR2 present in the ECM of non-tumorigenic organoids is sufficient, by itself, to disrupt cell polarization and organoid formation, thus leading to a disorganized phenotype with invasive properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing eAGR2 effects on polarity, lumen formation, and invasion in normal organoids.

claim: eAGR2 represents a novel and unexpected microenvironmental signaling in the epithelial morphogenesis and tumorigenesis which might be explored for development of novel therapeutic strategies for epithelial cancer.
source: Together, our results highlight that eAGR2 represents a novel and unexpected microenvironmental signaling in the epithelial morphogenesis and tumorigenesis which might be explored for development of novel therapeutic strategies for epithelial cancer.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing future therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: AGR2 encodes an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident protein mainly expressed in epithelial cells in human.
source: Anterior gradient 2 (AGR2) encodes an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident protein mainly expressed in epithelial cells in human.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about AGR2 localization and expression.

claim: Enhanced intracellular AGR2 (iAGR2) expression is observed in many cancers.
source: Enhanced intracellular AGR2 (iAGR2) expression is observed in many cancers (reviewed in Ref [Chevet et al., 2013]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: iAGR2 overexpression could represent a mechanistic intermediate between endoplasmic reticulum quality control (ERQC) and tumor development.
source: Previously, we have demonstrated that iAGR2 overexpression could represent a mechanistic intermediate between endoplasmic reticulum quality control (ERQC) and tumor development (Higa et al., 2011; Chevet et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: In cancer, AGR2 was present in the extracellular space, serum, and urine.
source: Although the iAGR2-mediated ER proteostasis control model is appealing, it was also observed that in cancer, AGR2 was present in the extracellular space, serum, and urine (Shi et al., 2014; Park et al., 2011), thereby opening other avenues for its role on tumor microenvironment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies detecting AGR2 in body fluids.

claim: AGR2 is a Protein-Disulfide Isomerase (PDI), PDIA17.
source: AGR2 is a Protein-Disulfide Isomerase (PDI), PDIA17 (Persson et al., 2005), and although the intracellular roles of PDIs have been well documented, some of these proteins were also found in the extracellular milieu, with unclear functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study classifying AGR2 as a PDI.

claim: PDIA2 is secreted into the lumen of the thyroid follicles by thyrocytes to control extracellular thyroglobulin folding and multimerisation.
source: For instance, we have previously shown that PDIA2 is secreted into the lumen of the thyroid follicles by thyrocytes to control extracellular thyroglobulin folding and multimerisation (Delom et al., 1999; Delom et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors on PDIA2.

claim: PDIA3 was found to be secreted and to interact with ECM proteins.
source: Further, PDIA3 was found to be secreted and to interact with ECM proteins (Dihazi et al., 2013) and QSOX1 was reported to participate in laminin assembly thereby controlling ECM functionality (Ilani et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on PDIA3 secretion and ECM interaction.

claim: QSOX1 was reported to participate in laminin assembly thereby controlling ECM functionality.
source: Further, PDIA3 was found to be secreted and to interact with ECM proteins (Dihazi et al., 2013) and QSOX1 was reported to participate in laminin assembly thereby controlling ECM functionality (Ilani et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on QSOX1 function in ECM assembly.

claim: Epithelial organization and many physiological cell-cell and cell-ECM contacts, cellular polarity, and secretory functions are preserved in epithelial organoids.
source: We and others, have recently demonstrated that epithelial organization and many physiological cell-cell and cell-ECM contacts, cellular polarity, and secretory functions are preserved in epithelial organoids (Fessart et al., 2013; Kimlin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on organoid models.

claim: The extracellular matrix (ECM) plays an instrumental role in determining the spatial orientation of epithelial polarity and the formation of lumens in glandular tissues during morphogenesis.
source: The extracellular matrix (ECM) plays an instrumental role in determining the spatial orientation of epithelial polarity and the formation of lumens in glandular tissues during morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ECM function in epithelial biology.

claim: AGR2 is an ER-resident protein involved in ER protein folding and quality control.
source: Here, we show that the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)-resident protein anterior gradient-2 (AGR2), a soluble protein-disulfide isomerase involved in ER protein folding and quality control, is secreted and interacts with the ECM.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about AGR2 function.

claim: AGR2 is secreted and interacts with the ECM.
source: Here, we show that the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)-resident protein anterior gradient-2 (AGR2), a soluble protein-disulfide isomerase involved in ER protein folding and quality control, is secreted and interacts with the ECM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing AGR2 in extracellular medium and ECM (Figure 5).

claim: Extracellular AGR2 (eAGR2) is a microenvironmental regulator of epithelial tissue architecture.
source: Extracellular AGR2 (eAGR2) is a microenvironmental regulator of epithelial tissue architecture, which plays a role in the preneoplastic phenotype and contributes to epithelial tumorigenicity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing eAGR2 effects on tissue organization and tumor properties.

claim: eAGR2 is secreted as a functionally active protein independently of its thioredoxin-like domain (CXXS) and of its ER-retention domain (KTEL).
source: Indeed, eAGR2, is secreted as a functionally active protein independently of its thioredoxin-like domain (CXXS) and of its ER-retention domain (KTEL), and is sufficient, by itself, to promote the acquisition of invasive and metastatic features.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with AGR2 mutants showing activity independent of CXXS and KTEL domains (Figure 6).

claim: eAGR2 is sufficient, by itself, to promote the acquisition of invasive and metastatic features.
source: Indeed, eAGR2, is secreted as a functionally active protein independently of its thioredoxin-like domain (CXXS) and of its ER-retention domain (KTEL), and is sufficient, by itself, to promote the acquisition of invasive and metastatic features.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing eAGR2 induces invasive phenotypes and EMT in normal organoids (Figures 7-9).

claim: eAGR2 plays an extracellular role independent of its ER function.
source: Therefore, we conclude that eAGR2 plays an extracellular role independent of its ER function and we elucidate this gain-of-function as a novel and unexpected critical ECM microenvironmental pro-oncogenic regulator of epithelial morphogenesis and tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing eAGR2 activity independent of ER-related domains and functions.

claim: Proper organization, maintenance, and function of the epithelial organs are largely ascribed to cell-cell adhesion and polarization of epithelium and its interaction with extracellular matrix (ECM).
source: It is well established that proper organization, maintenance, and function of the epithelial organs are largely ascribed to cell-cell adhesion and polarization of epithelium and its interaction with extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in epithelial biology.

claim: Apical-basal polarity is a fundamental feature of epithelial cells required for cell division, differentiation and morphogenesis.
source: Apical-basal polarity is a fundamental feature of epithelial cells required for cell division, differentiation and morphogenesis (Arumugam et al., 2008; Nelson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on epithelial polarity.

claim: Polarization is initiated by signaling from cell-to-cell and cell-to-ECM contacts.
source: Polarization is initiated by signaling from cell-to-cell and cell-to-ECM contacts (Nelson and Bissell, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on epithelial polarization.

claim: Loss of tissue organization is among the earliest hallmarks of epithelial cancer.
source: Conversely, loss of tissue organization is among the earliest hallmarks of epithelial cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cancer hallmarks.

claim: In extracellular medium from HEBC-AGR2 organoids, eAGR2 was detected but it was not O-glycosylated.
source: In the extracellular medium from HEBC-AGR2 organoids, eAGR2 was detected but it was not O-glycosylated (Figure 5-—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis for O-GlcNAc modification (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: AGR2 was demonstrated to be O-glycosylated upon secretion.
source: Recently, AGR2 was demonstrated to be O-glycosylated upon secretion (Clarke et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on AGR2 post-translational modification.

claim: The carboxyl-terminal KTEL domain is required for intracellular AGR2 enzymatic function.
source: It has been reported that the carboxyl-terminal KTEL domain is specifically required for intracellular AGR2 enzymatic function (Gupta et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on AGR2 domain function.

claim: AGR2 was found to interact with DAG1.
source: Indeed, AGR2 was found to interact with DAG1 (Fletcher et al., 2003), LYPD3 (Alanen et al., 2007), C4.4A (Arumugam et al., 2015), however the exact mechanisms by which AGR2 interacts with those proteins remains unclear and must be further investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on AGR2 protein interactions.

claim: AGR2 was found to interact with LYPD3.
source: Indeed, AGR2 was found to interact with DAG1 (Fletcher et al., 2003), LYPD3 (Alanen et al., 2007), C4.4A (Arumugam et al., 2015), however the exact mechanisms by which AGR2 interacts with those proteins remains unclear and must be further investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on AGR2 protein interactions.

claim: AGR2 was found to interact with C4.4A.
source: Indeed, AGR2 was found to interact with DAG1 (Fletcher et al., 2003), LYPD3 (Alanen et al., 2007), C4.4A (Arumugam et al., 2015), however the exact mechanisms by which AGR2 interacts with those proteins remains unclear and must be further investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on AGR2 protein interactions.

claim: Matrix MetalloProteinases (MMP) have been previously reported to play a critical role in stimulating invasion.
source: Matrix MetalloProteinases (MMP) have been previously reported to play a critical role in stimulating invasion (Kessenbrock et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on MMP function in invasion.

claim: Invasion of mesenchymal cells is enhanced by stiff ECM.
source: Since invasion of mesenchymal cells is enhanced by stiff ECM (Paszek and Weaver, 2004), we then assessed the impact of eAGR2 on the 3D-invasive potential in stiff ECM.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on ECM stiffness and invasion.

claim: AGR2 has been detected in the body fluids from cancer patients.
source: Since AGR2 has been detected in the body fluids from cancer patients (Chevet et al., 2013) as well as in the conditioned media from pancreatic and prostate cancer cells (Arumugam et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2005), we hypothesized that tumor organoids may also secrete AGR2 (extracellular AGR2 / eAGR2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies detecting AGR2 in body fluids.

claim: AGR2 has been detected in the conditioned media from pancreatic and prostate cancer cells.
source: Since AGR2 has been detected in the body fluids from cancer patients (Chevet et al., 2013) as well as in the conditioned media from pancreatic and prostate cancer cells (Arumugam et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2005), we hypothesized that tumor organoids may also secrete AGR2 (extracellular AGR2 / eAGR2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies detecting AGR2 in conditioned media.

claim: The average level of eAGR2 in the serum of cancer patients ranges from 0.5 to 20 ng/ml.
source: Given that eAGR2 is secreted by tumor organoids (Figure 5A) and that AGR2 has been reported in the serum of cancer patients with an average level of eAGR2 ranging from 0.5 to 20 ng/ml (Chen et al., 2010), we assessed whether eAGR2 might exhibit specific extracellular functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study measuring AGR2 levels in patient serum.

claim: Adherens junctions represent a powerful invasion suppressor complex in normal epithelial cells.
source: Adherens junctions represent a powerful invasion suppressor complex in normal epithelial cells (Pećina-Slaus, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on adherens junctions.

claim: MMPs play critical roles as they stimulate tumorigenesis, cancer cell invasion and metastasis.
source: In such context MMPs play critical roles as they stimulate tumorigenesis, cancer cell invasion and metastasis (Stallings-Mann et al., 2012; Arumugam et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on MMP function in cancer.

claim: MMP3 is critical for the cleavage of E-cadherin and is involved in promoting EMT and invasion in epithelial cells.
source: MMP9 may function to activate local growth factors, stimulate angiogenesis in vivo, and degrade the ECM during cell invasion, whereas MMP3 is critical for the cleavage of E-cadherin and is involved in promoting EMT and invasion in epithelial cells (Xian et al., 2005; Fingleton et al., 2001; Lochter et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on MMP3 function.

claim: EMT is a hallmark of tumor progression associated with the acquisition of invasive and metastatic features.
source: EMT is a hallmark of tumor progression associated with the acquisition of invasive and metastatic features (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a landmark review on cancer hallmarks.

claim: AGR2 has been correlated as potentially involved in EMT.
source: Since AGR2 has been correlated as potentially involved in EMT (Mizuuchi et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2015) and that EMT is characterized by a reduction of cell-cell adhesion and loss of apico-basolateral polarity (Thiery, 2002), we examined whether eAGR2 might regulate EMT in non-tumorigenic HBEC organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies correlating AGR2 with EMT.

claim: EMT is characterized by a reduction of cell-cell adhesion and loss of apico-basolateral polarity.
source: Since AGR2 has been correlated as potentially involved in EMT (Mizuuchi et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2015) and that EMT is characterized by a reduction of cell-cell adhesion and loss of apico-basolateral polarity (Thiery, 2002), we examined whether eAGR2 might regulate EMT in non-tumorigenic HBEC organoids.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on EMT characteristics.

claim: The synthesis and organization of ECM increases with time.
source: Since the synthesis and organization of ECM increases with time (Rashid et al., 2012), ECM was isolated after 8 days of culture (Figure 5L).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on ECM synthesis kinetics.

claim: Conditioned media from cells silenced for AGR2 have a reduced ability to stimulate proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells.
source: This is consistent with the observation that conditioned media from cells silenced for AGR2 have a reduced ability to stimulate proliferation of pancreatic cancer cells (Arumugam et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on AGR2 and cancer cell proliferation.

claim: Different affinities for the KDEL receptors may impact on subcellular distribution, the latter being dynamic and dependent on conditions such as cell density or growth media.
source: Recent studies have suggested that different affinities for the KDEL receptors may impact on subcellular distribution, the latter being dynamic and dependent on conditions such as cell density or growth media (Alanen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on KDEL receptor dynamics.

claim: A similar role for PDIA3 in remodeling of the ECM during renal fibrosis was described.
source: A similar role was described for PDIA3 in remodeling of the ECM during renal fibrosis (Dihazi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on PDIA3 function in ECM remodeling.
